plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: The 'This computer' section. It listed exact tool versions, how to reach WebGPU, and what to use in place of a pad, a phone or a second player, so I could run real experiments before committing the plan to anything. I also liked how it mixes freedom with firmness: genre, camera and engine changes are open, while the 10-foot UX, attract mode, dev mode and hub support are fixed. And STAGE.md being eight lines made the planner's job clear at once.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. First, 'Follow lib/hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': this could mean real multiplayer outside the hub, or only that the game must still work alone. The hub README points to the second reading, so I planned the same mode with AI rivals on its own, but I had to guess. Second, the tech stack: TASK.md says to build on dist/handoff, but that folder leaves out the 3D engine a first-person game needs. Its README step 7 sends you to the repository, while kits/README.md says a 3D game there is built on the 2D views. Third, TASK.md is written for the builder, so I had to work out which parts apply to the planner (package name, exit interview, Source Information, the model line) and write around file names that belong to this run only. Nothing said who the builders are or how long the plan should be, so I guessed at that too.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: On design, capturing what makes the source distinctive without recreating it. Each signature idea needed its own original form: salt-dust lung instead of malaria, a dying hydrologist and her depth logbooks instead of the arms dealer and his tapes, a flood ending instead of the source's. They still had to deliver the same pressure and mood. On scope, writing one plan with enough detail and a safe cut order for builders of very different capability. On the technical side, the hub check: a 3D page that boots in about 4 s alone took 20.8 s as four copies on one thread and failed the harness's 20 s ready wait. Finding a boot order that passes took real runs. The fire system was the other risk, and I prototyped it on both WebGL 2 and WebGPU before writing it down.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: Say plainly what multiplayer 'on its own' requires. State that a 3D game takes engine/my-3d2dge-3d.js, vendor/ and src/starter3d/ from the repository, or put them in the handoff package. Give the planner the builders' models and effort levels, a target demo length and a rough size limit for the plan. Mark which TASK.md sections are builder-only, so the planner can skip them. Add one line on hub boot timing: call connect() early and ready() before any heavy warm-up, because the 20 s ready wait with all copies on one main thread appears only in the harness source, not in the protocol README, and any 3D game will hit it.
